news.content_title: Rabies vaccine hesitancy a recurring topic for NH veterinarians, legislators
news.content: For household dogs, cats and ferrets, rabies is the only vaccine required by New Hampshire state law. (Photo by Sebastian Condrea/Getty Images) Last month, the House Environment and Agriculture Committee recommended reconsidering the contents of a sidelined bill from last session: House Bill 1488 , which sought to increase rabies vaccine exemptions for New Hampshire pets. The bill was sent for interim study by the full New Hampshire House in March and, with the 2026 session closed and the biennium winding down, was no longer eligible for passage. Instead, the committee voted, 10-1, to recommend the topic be addressed in future legislation. That move came as a surprise to some. "Truthfully, we didn't think it was going to go as far," said Dr. Jane Barlow Roy, who chairs the legislative committee of the New Hampshire Veterinary Medical Association. That's because there is broad consensus among veterinarians that the rabies vaccine — which protects against a disease both transmissible to humans and universally fatal — is safe and life-saving. Yet the bill was driven forward by pet owners concerned about the rare but non-zero occurrence of adverse reactions to the vaccine, reflecting the increasing hesitancy around both human and pet shots that is driving the resurgence of some infectious diseases in the U.S. Committee members said at an October work session they wanted to keep the door open to potential future changes to rabies vaccine guidance and ensure the topic is revisited if more information becomes available. But answering some of the questions raised by pet owners and legislators, veterinarians said, will require research that is complicated and ethically fraught. For household dogs, cats and ferrets, rabies is the only vaccine required by New Hampshire state law. The viral illness is transmitted when saliva from an infected animal touches broken skin or mucous membranes like those inside the mouth, nose and eyes. The virus moves slowly through nervous tissue, incubating for weeks or more before symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, vomiting, and, later, aggression, difficulty swallowing or paralysis begin to manifest. While post-exposure treatment can prevent the disease from progressing if it is administered soon enough, once symptoms appear, the disease is considered incurable. Wildlife are the most common transmitters of rabies in the U.S., where the prevalence of vaccines has reduced both the disease's incidence in domestic animals and the rabies death rate in humans and pets. But globally, about 70,000 people die of rabies each year, and more than 99% of people who get the disease outside the U.S. are infected by a dog , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In the U.S., there was an unusually high number of human exposures documented this year, according to the CDC. And recent research suggests that the disease is responsible for more human deaths nationwide than scientists once believed. Kelly Arsenault, a Sandown Realtor, is skeptical about some vaccines. But rabies, she said, is not one that she skips when she brings her small dogs to the vet. "I believe in the ability of the body to heal," she said. "However, rabies is not one of them — and I know that — it is not one of those that the body is going to heal from." Yet Arsenault, who has for years worked to help rehome and rescue small dogs, also has questions about the rabies vaccine. More than 150 dogs, most of them fluffy and weighing under 15 pounds, have passed through Arsenault's care over the years, she said. To date, one that she is aware of has had a significant negative reaction to a vaccine, she said, becoming severely ill after injection. Treating the dog with allergy medication managed the reaction, she said, but it was unsettling. She wonders why it happened and whether the incident could have been prevented. Negative reactions to vaccines in pets are uncommon, but most often appear similar to what many people experience after a flu shot, like injection site soreness and mild discomfort, said Dr. Lisa Boyer, a Seacoast area veterinarian, in an online seminar this October. Less commonly, severe reactions can involve facial swelling, vomiting or difficulty breathing. These reactions are managed with veterinary care, said Barlow Roy. And in New Hampshire, as in some other states, a pathway exists in state law to allow owners of pets susceptible to reactions to seek an exemption from the requirement. "The process is there for those dogs and cats that truly should not be getting the rabies vaccine," said Barlow Roy. That exemption must be approved by the New Hampshire state veterinarian; after it is granted, exempt animals must be kept away from other animals or muzzled. Owners also assume more liability for their unvaccinated animals. For these reasons and the lethal nature of the rabies virus, the veterinarians consider the vaccine more than worthwhile for almost all pets. Yet the online proliferation of information and misinformation about vaccines has raised more curiosity among pet owners, who are asking more questions and starting conversations the veterinarians said they welcomed. However, in some cases, they said, pet owners have also become more likely to push back against professionals' recommendations. HB 1488 sought to broaden the allowed cases for rabies vaccine exemptions in New Hampshire under one condition: A pet has received a series of tests attempting to demonstrate that their immune system has responded to the vaccine. Those tests, known as antibody titers, can measure the level of rabies-specific antibodies, or immune system proteins, in a pet's blood. The pet's own white blood cells produce antibodies after they are exposed to the inactivated virus molecules in a vaccine; then the antibodies remain in the pet's blood, ready to raise the alarm if they ever encounter the rabies virus again, such as if the pet is exposed to rabies from a wild animal. The idea of a titer testing protocol appeals to Arsenault, she said, because if a test could demonstrate that her pet is protected against rabies, she could skip additional "booster" shots. But the problem, according to veterinarians, is that there is currently no test that can prove definitively whether or not a pet has enough antibodies to be protected against rabies. If a titer comes back showing rabies antibodies in a pet's blood, that confirms that the animal has some degree of immunity against rabies from a previous vaccination, Barlow Roy said. But it takes a certain threshold amount of antibodies to actually combat the virus in the case of a real exposure. That makes the rabies titer test unhelpful for two reasons. One limitation, according to American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jennifer Quammen, is that the test is a snapshot in time of a dynamic situation. The amount of antibodies in a pet's blood changes as time goes on; this is part of the reason booster shots are called for. Second, scientists don't have a reliable way of knowing what threshold amount of antibodies a pet's blood must contain in order for them to be fully protected against the rabies virus. Therefore, in the face of a deadly disease like rabies, veterinarians recommend pets get boosters on schedule to ensure they are protected. The limitation of the rabies titer test doesn't apply to some other diseases for which scientists have developed titer testing protocol. Pet owners may opt to use an antibody titer test to guide decisions about booster shots for some other illnesses, like canine distemper and parvovirus, veterinarians said. With rabies, the factor that has limited the development of a titer testing protocol is the disease's lethality. Reaching a conclusion about what level of blood antibodies is enough to protect a dog requires testing on living animals. Dogs with different levels of antibodies in their blood, for example, would be intentionally exposed to the disease; some are expected to contract the illness. That result helps scientists determine how much antibody is actually protective. Animals that contract diseases for which treatments exist can be supported after that experiment with medical intervention, Barlow Roy said, making these studies less problematic for investigators. But an animal that begins showing signs of rabies is effectively facing a death sentence, making the protocol more fraught. "We're not comparing apples to apples, you know? We're in the same realm," she said, describing the differences in rabies titer research versus that on other diseases. "It's more challenging from an ethical point of view ... and that's why we hesitate," she said. Arsenault said she was conflicted: While she wants the results of the experiment, she also feels moral qualms about what it would necessitate. "That's probably where this whole thing gets difficult," she said. "Would I be willing to be part of that study and watch a dog die from rabies? No ... I don't know if I could live with myself." However, some advocates of reducing rabies vaccine frequency have pushed for that research to move ahead, and some studies of limited scope have been completed. That included a 2020 study funded by the Rabies Challenge Fund Charitable Trust that involved the euthanasia of at least 45 beagles, some of which were infected with rabies, raising objections from animal rights groups like People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. But research has not yielded enough data to draw conclusions, veterinarians told legislators at hearings on HB 1488. Most rabies policy and vaccine guidance is based on a document called the "rabies compendium," compiled by the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians. The document is due for revision this year, said Dr. Nathan Harvey, New Hampshire assistant state veterinarian, at an October work session on the bill. Veterinarians expect that the compendium will include updated guidance on the vaccine, possibly — but not certainly — to include guidance around the use of titer testing. "They are looking at whether or not we can start making those correlations to (titer levels) being protective, and that information may come out in the compendium. But we can't assume that information is going to be published, or not," Barlow Roy said. The reality at present continues to be that titer tests cannot replace vaccine programs, for the sake of animal and human health, Quammen said. Some pet owners have also raised concerns about particularly small animals, like the dogs that Arsenault rescues. Some negative reactions seem to occur with more frequency in small animals, Barlow Roy said, though she stressed that they are still uncommon. But while pet owners like Arsenault have asked whether a smaller "dose" of vaccine could be administered to smaller animals, that is misleading, Boyer said. Confusion can arise, she said, because many medications are dosed by body weight. But the way that vaccines work — by triggering an immune response — is not as sensitive to body size, meaning that the amount of a vaccine's active ingredient that an animal must receive for the vaccine to work is not necessarily different for, say, a Pomeranian and a Lab. "If you cut the dose in half and assume you have an appropriate dose, you will not be fully vaccinated or fully protected," she said. But there are other components besides dead viral molecules in a vaccine, and some formulations exist that deliver the same amount of active ingredient in a smaller volume, Boyer said. Veterinarians continue to recommend the rabies booster schedule that is widely accepted as the safest and best option for people and pets. South Acworth Republican Rep. Judy Aron, who chaired the House Committee on Environment and Agriculture last session but did not seek reelection this fall, said during the Oct. 6 work session that the topic could be revisited by the Legislature if more guidance is released in the revised compendium. Barlow Roy urged pet owners to discuss any concerns with their veterinarian, including by reporting any incidences of suspected vaccine side effects, which she said clinics routinely share with vaccine manufacturers. For Barlow Roy, the urgency of keeping pets protected from the virus is augmented by her compassion for the animals that visit her exam table — and the humans who love them. "If I ever, God forbid, have an animal in my care that has rabies and it is given to, you know, a child in the household, or another family member, a human, that we could have prevented, that would definitely crush me," she said. "That's always the thing in the back of my head: Rabies is 100% fatal. It results in death 100% of the time. I think that's why we are so adamant about rabies and this whole titer discussion." But it takes a certain threshold amount of antibodies to actually combat the virus in the case of a real exposure. That makes the rabies titer test unhelpful for two reasons. One limitation, according to American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jennifer Quammen, is that the test is a snapshot in time of a dynamic situation. The amount of antibodies in a pet's blood changes as time goes on; this is part of the reason booster shots are called for. Second, scientists don't have a reliable way of knowing what threshold amount of antibodies a pet's blood must contain in order for them to be fully protected against the rabies virus. Therefore, in the face of a deadly disease like rabies, veterinarians recommend pets get boosters on schedule to ensure they are protected. The limitation of the rabies titer test doesn't apply to some other diseases for which scientists have developed titer testing protocol. Pet owners may opt to use an antibody titer test to guide decisions about booster shots for some other illnesses, like canine distemper and parvovirus, veterinarians said. With rabies, the factor that has limited the development of a titer testing protocol is the disease's lethality. Reaching a conclusion about what level of blood antibodies is enough to protect a dog requires testing on living animals. Dogs with different levels of antibodies in their blood, for example, would be intentionally exposed to the disease; some are expected to contract the illness. That result helps scientists determine how much antibody is actually protective. Animals that contract diseases for which treatments exist can be supported after that experiment with medical intervention, Barlow Roy said, making these studies less problematic for investigators. But an animal that begins showing signs of rabies is effectively facing a death sentence, making the protocol more fraught. "We're not comparing apples to apples, you know? We're in the same realm," she said, describing the differences in rabies titer research versus that on other diseases. "It's more challenging from an ethical point of view ... and that's why we hesitate," she said. Arsenault said she was conflicted: While she wants the results of the experiment, she also feels moral qualms about what it would necessitate. "That's probably where this whole thing gets difficult," she said. "Would I be willing to be part of that study and watch a dog die from rabies? No ... I don't know if I could live with myself." However, some advocates of reducing rabies vaccine frequency have pushed for that research to move ahead, and some studies of limited scope have been completed. That included a 2020 study funded by the Rabies Challenge Fund Charitable Trust that involved the euthanasia of at least 45 beagles, some of which were infected with rabies, raising objections from animal rights groups like People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. But research has not yielded enough data to draw conclusions, veterinarians told legislators at hearings on HB 1488. Most rabies policy and vaccine guidance is based on a document called the "rabies compendium," compiled by the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians. The document is due for revision this year, said Dr. Nathan Harvey, New Hampshire assistant state veterinarian, at an October work session on the bill. Veterinarians expect that the compendium will include updated guidance on the vaccine, possibly — but not certainly — to include guidance around the use of titer testing. "They are looking at whether or not we can start making those correlations to (titer levels) being protective, and that information may come out in the compendium. But we can't assume that information is going to be published, or not," Barlow Roy said. The reality at present continues to be that titer tests cannot replace vaccine programs, for the sake of animal and human health, Quammen said. Some pet owners have also raised concerns about particularly small animals, like the dogs that Arsenault rescues. Some negative reactions seem to occur with more frequency in small animals, Barlow Roy said, though she stressed that they are still uncommon. But while pet owners like Arsenault have asked whether a smaller "dose" of vaccine could be administered to smaller animals, that is misleading, Boyer said. Confusion can arise, she said, because many medications are dosed by body weight. But the way that vaccines work — by triggering an immune response — is not as sensitive to body size, meaning that the amount of a vaccine's active ingredient that an animal must receive for the vaccine to work is not necessarily different for, say, a Pomeranian and a Lab. "If you cut the dose in half and assume you have an appropriate dose, you will not be fully vaccinated or fully protected," she said. But there are other components besides dead viral molecules in a vaccine, and some formulations exist that deliver the same amount of active ingredient in a smaller volume, Boyer said. Veterinarians continue to recommend the rabies booster schedule that is widely accepted as the safest and best option for people and pets. South Acworth Republican Rep. Judy Aron, who chaired the House Committee on Environment and Agriculture last session but did not seek reelection this fall, said during the Oct. 6 work session that the topic could be revisited by the Legislature if more guidance is released in the revised compendium. Barlow Roy urged pet owners to discuss any concerns with their veterinarian, including by reporting any incidences of suspected vaccine side effects, which she said clinics routinely share with vaccine manufacturers. For Barlow Roy, the urgency of keeping pets protected from the virus is augmented by her compassion for the animals that visit her exam table — and the humans who love them. "If I ever, God forbid, have an animal in my care that has rabies and it is given to, you know, a child in the household, or another family member, a human, that we could have prevented, that would definitely crush me," she said. "That's always the thing in the back of my head: Rabies is 100% fatal. It results in death 100% of the time. I think that's why we are so adamant about rabies and this whole titer discussion." news.title_zh: 狂犬病 疫苗 疑虑是新罕布什尔州兽医和立法者反复讨论的话题
news.source_body_en: For household dogs, cats and ferrets, rabies is the only vaccine required by New Hampshire state law. (Photo by Sebastian Condrea/Getty Images) Last month, the House Environment and Agriculture Committee recommended reconsidering the contents of a sidelined bill from last session: House Bill 1488 , which sought to increase rabies vaccine exemptions for New Hampshire pets. The bill was sent for interim study by the full New Hampshire House in March and, with the 2026 session closed and the biennium winding down, was no longer eligible for passage. Instead, the committee voted, 10-1, to recommend the topic be addressed in future legislation. That move came as a surprise to some. "Truthfully, we didn't think it was going to go as far," said Dr. Jane Barlow Roy, who chairs the legislative committee of the New Hampshire Veterinary Medical Association.
news.content_zh: 对于家庭犬、猫和水貂,新罕布什尔州法律要求仅需疫苗 狂犬病。(照片由Sebastian Condrea/Getty Images提供) 上个月,众议院环境与农业委员会建议重新考虑上一届会议搁置的一项法案的内容:众议院法案1488号,该法案旨在增加新罕布什尔州宠物的疫苗 狂犬病豁免。该法案于三月份被发送至全州众议院进行中期研究,并随着2026届会议的结束和任期的临近尾声,该法案已不再具备通过的资格。相反,委员会以10比1的投票结果建议将该议题纳入未来的立法中。这一举措令一些人感到意外。新罕布什尔州兽医医学协会立法委员会主席简·巴洛·罗伊博士表示:"说实话,我们没想到它会发展到这种程度。"

analysis.time: November 3rd, 2026 (publication date), 1 day ago (event date) [N1, N35].
analysis.event: Merck Animal Health launched nonadjuvanted rabies vaccines for dogs and cats due to rising human exposures. The event is reported by Caitlin McCafferty, Content Producer [N35].
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The CDC warned of a nationwide increase in reported human rabies exposures, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided in the evidence [N35].
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The launch of vaccines is a response to the increased risk of human rabies exposures, but the status of the investigation or any specific actions taken is not detailed in the evidence [N35].

analysis.brief_en: Merck Animal Health has launched nonadjuvanted rabies vaccines for dogs and cats in response to a nationwide increase in reported human rabies exposures, as highlighted by the CDC. The development of these vaccines comes weeks after the CDC issued a warning about the rising trend of human rabies cases. The article, published on November 3rd, 2026, by Caitlin McCafferty, Content Producer, notes that the vaccines are available in 1-year and 3-year formulations. While the article emphasizes the growing concern for human rabies exposures, it does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. The response to this situation involves the introduction of new vaccines, but the article does not detail the investigation status or any other specific actions taken. This development is part of broader efforts to address rabies prevention in veterinary care, with no mention of related viruses or hard exclusions.

Search for: Andaman Live Videos Home Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Andaman Media Delegation Visits Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor; Experts Share Insights on Rabies Prevention for Andaman and Vaccine Research Sanjib Posted on 8 months ago Spread the love Sheekha Bureau Coonoor, March 13: A delegation of media representatives from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the historic Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor on 12 March as part of a study tour aimed at understanding the institute’s work in vaccine research, manufacturing and disease prevention. The visit provided the delegation with an opportunity to learn about the institute’s scientific activities and its long-standing contribution to vaccine development in the country. During the visit, officials of the institute briefed the delegation about its research programmes, vaccine manufacturing processes and the role it has played in producing vaccines for major infectious diseases. The delegation also interacted with Dr. S. Sivakumar is the Director of the Pasteur Institute of India and senior scientists, who explained how vaccines were produced in the past and how the institute plans to expand its manufacturing capabilities in the coming years. One of the key topics discussed during the interaction was rabies, a viral disease that affects all warm-blooded animals and is mainly transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, most commonly through dog bites. Experts at the institute explained that once the rabies virus enters the body, it travels through the nervous system to the brain, where it multiplies and damages neural tissue. Once the central nervous system is affected, survival chances are extremely low, making prevention and timely treatment crucial. The experts also spoke about the situation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where rabies has not been reported so far. They advised that strict precautions must be maintained to keep the islands rabies-free. According to them, authorities should ensure that any animals brought from the mainland, particularly dogs and cats, are properly vaccinated and accompanied by valid vaccination certificates from recognized institutions. Proper verification of such certificates is essential before allowing animals to enter the islands. The scientists also highlighted the importance of immediate first aid in the event of an animal bite. Washing the wound thoroughly with plenty of water and seeking prompt medical attention for anti-rabies treatment can significantly reduce the risk of infection. The Pasteur Institute of India, located in Coonoor in Tamil Nadu, is one of the country’s premier government institutions dedicated to vaccine research and production. Functioning as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, the institute has played a pioneering role in the development and supply of vaccines for several decades. The institute traces its origins to 1907, when it was established as the Pasteur Institute of Southern India following the death of a young woman who could not receive timely anti-rabies treatment. Over the years, it has achieved several milestones in vaccine research and manufacturing, including the production of anti-rabies vaccines, influenza vaccines and oral polio vaccines. In 2001, the institute developed a purified rabies vaccine derived from Vero cells for human use at an affordable cost, becoming the first government-controlled institution in India to do so. The move significantly helped reduce the cost of rabies vaccines in the country. Today, the institute operates modern facilities for the production of DPT group vaccines and has an installed capacity of around 130 million doses. Its laboratories are equipped with advanced technology and equipment used for large-scale vaccine production and research. The institute is also involved in academic activities, including doctoral research in microbiology, biochemistry and biotechnology. In addition, its anti-rabies treatment centre, established in 1907, continues to treat animal bite cases and collect important epidemiological data. Looking ahead, the institute plans to expand its capabilities further by establishing new biosafety level facilities for the production of viral, bacterial, conjugate and recombinant DNA vaccines. These developments are expected to strengthen India’s vaccine security and preparedness for future public health challenges. The visit provided the Andaman media delegation with valuable insights into vaccine research and public health preparedness, particularly in understanding the importance of maintaining strict preventive measures to keep regions like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands free from rabies. analysis_en.location_and_population: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Coonoor, Tamil Nadu, India.
analysis_en.event: A media delegation from Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor to learn about rabies prevention and vaccine research. The visit was aimed at understanding the institute’s work in vaccine research, manufacturing, and disease prevention.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The delegation learned about the institute’s research programs, vaccine manufacturing processes, and the role it has played in producing vaccines for major infectious diseases. The experts advised maintaining strict precautions to keep the islands rabies-free, emphasizing the importance of immediate first aid and proper animal vaccination.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The institute plans to expand its capabilities by establishing new biosafety level facilities for the production of viral, bacterial, conjugate, and recombinant DNA vaccines. The visit provided valuable insights into vaccine research and public health preparedness.

news.source_body_en: A media delegation from Andaman and Nicobar Islands visited the Pasteur Institute of India in Coonoor to learn about rabies prevention and vaccine research. Experts at the institute briefed the delegation on vaccine manufacturing processes and the importance of maintaining strict preventive measures to keep the islands rabies-free. They emphasized the need for immediate first aid and proper animal vaccination.

news.content_title: 狂犬病毒的分类学(七)_腾讯新闻
news.content: 前记 : 目前国际上关于狂犬病研究最权威、最全面的大型学术专著是 《 狂犬病的科学基础和管控( RABIES: SCIENTIFIC BASIS OF THE DISEASE AND ITS MANAGEMENT) 》,简称《 狂犬病 (RABIES) 》。该专著最新版( 第 5 版 )已于 2025年7月 面世。 本公众号已陆续将该专著第 4版(2020年版)的绝大部分内容翻译成中文。该专著最新版对旧版有较 多更新和 改进。本公众号将继续全文翻译该专著最新版的内容 , 将优先翻译新增加或更新较多章节的内容。 以下为该专著最新版 新增加的一章: 第 2 章 分类学 ( Taxonomy ) ( 七 ) 作者: Noël Tordo, Peter J. Walker 2.7 物种名称的逐步演变 ( The progressive evolution of the species names ) 按照惯例,病毒通常由首次描述它们的人命名,或依据其后在科学文献中形成的共识命名。就 狂犬病毒属 病毒而言,各自的命名遵循着颇为多样的逻辑:疾病(狂犬病, rabies );分离地点 / 地区( Mokola virus 、 Aravan virus 、 Duvenhage virus 、 Ikoma lyssavirus 等);分离地点 / 地区与宿主( Bokeloh bat lyssavirus 、 West Caucasian bat lyssavirus 等);分离的洲与宿主( Australian bat lyssavirus 、 European bat lyssavirus 1 等)。 病毒名称不受 ICTV 任何决定的约束,因为 ICTV 的职权仅涉及病毒分类单元的创设与命名,以及将病毒归入这些分类单元 (Mayo, 2002) 。在 ICTV 于 1991 年决定将病毒物种确立为最低分类阶元之后,最初是直接采用 病毒名称 来同时代表 物种名称 。然而许多人认为这种做法容易造成混淆,因为它未能充分区分 病毒(具象实体 )与相应的 物种(病毒被归入的抽象分类学范畴 )。这在病毒学家中引发了多年的大量争论,而 ICTV 随后的一系列决定逐步形成了当前所用的病毒物种名称。 a. 1998 年,各方同意保留现有的 物种名称 (等同于病毒名称),但应将其排为斜体并首字母大写,遵循既有的更高阶病毒分类单元 —— 属、科和目 —— 的惯例 (Adams et al., 2017) 。该命名体系所需改动最小,并首次在 2005 年 ICTV 第八次报告中用于所有病毒物种( Virus Taxonomy, 8th Report of the ICTV )。 b. 在随后的数年中, ICTV 进而转向在物种名称中纳入属名 (van Regenmortel et al., 2010) 。这在很大程度上交由各研究组自行落实, 弹状病毒科 研究组最终采纳了这一做法。于是,例如 Rabies virus 物种变为 Rabies lyssavirus , Mokola virus 物种变为 Mokola lyssavirus ;但对于 European bat lyssavirus 1 这类名称中已包含属名的物种,其物种名称则保持不变。这一做法首次采用于 2018 年 ICTV 第十次报告 (Walker et al., 2018) 。 c. 2021 年,代表病毒学各领域(动物、植物、细菌和古菌)众多病毒学家的 ICTV 全体成员以压倒性多数投票通过, 对所有病毒物种实施标准的 双名法命名 (Walker et al., 2021) 。这是经过数年考量和公开辩论后作出的决定,其主要目的是确保病毒分类学命名在各科之间更加一致,并更贴合生物学其他分支所采用的林奈系统。根据这一现已强制实施的命名法, 病毒物种名称必须排为斜体,且必须由两个词构成 ,第一个词为属名,第二个词为称作 种加词 ( species epithet )的唯一标识符。每个词均排为斜体,且仅属名以大写字母开头。与生物学其他分支一样,种加词可以拉丁化,但对病毒而言并非强制。拟用种加词的选择交由各研究组决定。在弹状病毒科研究组中,植物病毒学家成员投票赞成使用拉丁化的种加词;而动物病毒学家则选择逐案采用拉丁化或非拉丁化的种加词,并尽可能保留与病毒名称的关联。于是,例如 Rabies lyssavirus 物种变为 Lyssavirus rabies , Mokola lyssavirus 物种变为 Lyssavirus mokola , European bat lyssavirus 1 物种变为 Lyssavirus hamburg (以首次分离地命名)。 修订后的物种名称于 2022 年获得批准,首次出现在 2023 年 ICTV 报告的在线修订版中 (Walker et al., 2022b) 。 表 2.1 概括了从最初的狂犬病毒属物种名称到现行名称的这一渐进演变。尽管这一演变对 ICTV 而言是必要的,以便更合乎逻辑地对通过高通量测序鉴定出的呈指数增长的新病毒进行分类,但它也造成了一些混淆。其中很大一部分源于许多人未能理解病毒与其所归入的物种之间的区别,也未能认识到病毒名称本身始终未变 (Zerbini et al., 2022) 。狂犬病病毒仍然是狂犬病病毒,在讨论该病毒时应始终以此称之。此外,狂犬病病毒公认的缩写( RABV )同样保持不变,且应仅在指称病毒时使用,而不用于指称病毒物种。事实上,在多数情况下,狂犬病病毒(或任何其他病毒)的分类学归属只需提及一次即可,即:狂犬病病毒( RABV )在分类学上归入弹状病毒科、狂犬病毒属、 Lyssavirus rabies 物种。或者表述为: 狂犬病病毒( RABV ,物种 Lyssavirus rabies )是一种在分类学上归入弹状病毒科、单股负链病毒目的弹状病毒。此后,在报告有关该病毒的数据、实验或观察结果时,可使用狂犬病病毒(注意不大写首字母,因其并非专有名词)或其缩写( RABV )。 值得思考的是,病毒分类学就其本质而言是一幅不断变动的挂毯。随着已知 病毒圈( virosphere ) 的持续扩展,以及我们不断开发出用以认识病毒及其进化和生态关系的工具,我们的分类系统及其分类学归属也在演进。 ICTV 力求逐步实现稳定的分类,但它终究是一部人为构建的目录,而如何最好地管理它,将永远是病毒学家争论的议题。归根结底, 病毒名称的稳定性,以及对病毒与病毒物种之间区别的充分了解,将有助于避免不必要的混淆 。 (本章全文完) 本公众号相关文章的链接 news.content: News Sports Entertainment Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Oneida County Health Dept: Another animal tests positive for rabies Amy Neff Roth Utica Observer Dispatch Updated Nov. 4, 2026, 4:47 p.m. ET A raccoon in Vernon has tested positive for rabies, the Oneida County Health Department announced. Two dogs may have been exposed to the raccoon and received rabies booster shots. So far this year 11 animals have tested positive in the county; they may have exposed 13 people, four dogs and a cat; one unvaccinatd dog had to be placed in quarantine. Another raccoon has tested positive for rabies in Oneida County, this one in Vernon, according to the Oneida County Health Department. The raccoon was sent for testing on Nov. 3 and the positive results were reported back to the county health department on Nov. 4. Two dogs previously vaccinated against rabies were exposed to the raccoon; both received booster shots. This was the fifth raccoon in the county to test positive for rabies this year. The others were found in Deansboro in October, in Westmoreland in August, in Whitesboro in July and in Westmoreland in May. In total, the health department has reported 11 positive rabies tests this year. The others were for four bats (in South Utica in September, in Chadwicks in August, in New Hartford in July and in Rome in April); and two foxes (in Whitesboro in May and in Camden in April). In the 10 earlier cases, 13 people were exposed to the animal with rabies and needed preventative shots. And four dogs and a cat were also exposed; three of the dogs and the cat had previously been vaccinated against rabies and just needed booster shots. The fourth dog was unvaccinated and had to be placed in quarantine. Last year Oneida County sent 170 animals to the New York State Department of Health’s Wadsworth Center for rabies testing, according to the state health department. Ten of those samples tested positive for rabies, including four bats, one cat, one fox, three raccoons and one skunk. Bats were the animal most often sent for testing with 106 samples compared to 30 samples for the second most common animal sent for testing, cats. Seven animals tested positive for rabies in Madison County last year, including three raccoons, two cats, a skunk and an animal only described as “wild other,” according to state data. (That means it was not a bat, fox, raccoon, rodent or skunk, which are listed individually in the report.) No animals tested positive for rabies in Herkimer County last year, according to the state health department. Signs of rabies Signs of rabies in animals include strange, shy or “mad” behavior; an animal getting unusually close; or drooling or foaming from the mouth, according to the county health department. Stay away from any animals, whether they are wild or stray, exhibiting these signs, public health officials warn. Call your local animal control officer or local police department. The health department also suggested other resources that may be able to help: A licensed nuisance wildlife control operator. Find one here on the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation website. A licensed wildlife rehabilitator. Find one here on the DEC website. The NY DEC online or at 1-844-332-3267. Environmental conservation officers. Find one here on the DEC site. If a person or pet may have been exposed to an animal with rabies, contact the county health department at 315-798-5064 at any time. New York State Law requires pet owners to get all dogs, cats and ferrets vaccinated against rabies by the time they’re four months old and then one year after the first dose. Ferrets need annual booster shots. Dog and cats need boosters every three years after the first two shots. The Oneida County Health Department is no longer offering rabies vaccine clinics this year, but it will begin offering them again in 2027. news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Numerous deaths from rabies: Doctors warn of mistakes in prevention. (Dan Tri Newspaper) - Many deaths have been attributed to rabies after people were bitten by dogs but did not receive the vaccine. Doctors warn that rabies has a nearly 100% mortality rate once symptoms appear. Find Pet Care Báo Dân trí•03/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Recently, the Dong Nai City Center for Disease Control (CDC Dong Nai) announced that the locality had recorded a death due to rabies, following a bite from a dog suspected of having rabies about two months ago. All the patients who died had not received a vaccine after being bitten by a dog. The patient was Mr. D.G. (27 years old, residing in Dong Nai City). This is the fourth death due to rabies in the city since the beginning of the year. According to the Dong Nai CDC, about two months ago, Mr. G. was bitten on the finger by a stray dog. He then killed the dog. The patient did not treat the wound and did not get vaccinated against rabies. On October 15th, Mr. G. began experiencing symptoms such as fever, chills, fatigue, loss of appetite, difficulty swallowing, and later became unable to eat or drink. On October 18th, when his symptoms did not improve, Mr. G. was taken to a medical facility and then transferred to the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases. There, he was diagnosed with rabies. Due to the severity of his condition, his family requested to take him home, and he died at home. Find Pet Care Previously, on September 11th, Gia Lai Provincial Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital reported the death of KS, a 6-year-old child, due to rabies after being bitten by dogs twice without receiving the rabies vaccine. About five months ago, the child was bitten on the leg by a neighbor's dog. Two months later, the child was bitten on the ear by another stray dog. However, on both occasions, the family did not take the child to a medical facility for wound treatment or rabies vaccination. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Vaccines Book Vet Visits On September 6th, the child appeared tired and lethargic. The following morning, the child had seizures and was rushed to the emergency room before being transferred to the Gia Lai Provincial Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital. There, doctors diagnosed rabies. The family requested to take the child home, where the child subsequently died. Find Pet Care A young man died of rabies two months after being bitten by a dog, without receiving a rabies vaccine (Photo: Getty). Find Pet Care About two months ago, the Department of Health of Dong Thap province reported the case of a 4-year-old girl, NPAN, residing in Dao Thanh ward, who died from rabies after allegedly being bitten by a dog. According to the investigation, on July 4th, while visiting her maternal grandparents in My Phuoc Tay ward, the child suddenly started crying loudly. The family discovered a wound about 6cm long on the child's forehead, bleeding profusely. A dog ran nearby, but it could not be determined whether the child had been bitten by the dog. The child was taken to a local hospital to have the wound stitched up. Because the family did not report a suspected dog bite, the child was not advised to receive rabies vaccine and antiserum. The next day, the family took the child to a vaccination center for consultation, but they refused to administer the rabies vaccine. On August 13th, the child was hospitalized in critical condition, experiencing seizures and motor disturbances. After several transfers to other hospitals, doctors discovered suspected dog bite marks on the forehead. Notably, two saliva tests both returned positive results for the rabies virus. You may also like The child's condition continued to worsen, and he was diagnosed with aggressive rabies, accompanied by respiratory failure and numerous complications. On the evening of August 22nd, the family requested to take the child home. The child died at home that same day. Find Pet Care 100% mortality rate once symptoms appear. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), rabies is a dangerous infectious disease caused by a virus, transmitted from animals to humans. The disease has a nearly 100% mortality rate once clinical symptoms appear, but it is completely preventable if treated and vaccinated promptly after exposure. Each year, rabies claims the lives of tens of thousands of people worldwide . Notably, approximately 40% of victims are children under 15 years old. Dogs are the primary source of rabies virus transmission, accounting for about 99% of human rabies cases. Rabies can infect all mammals, from common pets like dogs, cats, and cattle to wild animals. The rabies virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the saliva of infected animals, most commonly through bites or scratches. The virus can also enter the body when the saliva of an infected animal comes into direct contact with the mucous membranes of the eyes, mouth, or open wounds. The incubation period for rabies typically lasts from two to three months, but can range from one week to one year. This timeframe depends on several factors, including the location of the wound, the extent of the injury, and the amount of virus that enters the body. In the early stages, the disease often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, pain, or an unusual tingling, stinging, or burning sensation at the wound site. When the virus spreads to the central nervous system, the patient may develop encephalitis or myelitis, and the condition can quickly become critical. Find Treatments Rabies in humans is generally divided into two main forms. The aggressive form can cause hyperactivity, agitation, hallucinations, hydrophobia, aerophobia, and unusual behavioral changes. Patients usually die within a few days due to cardiac or respiratory arrest. Meanwhile, paralytic rabies accounts for about 20% of human rabies cases. This form of the disease usually progresses more slowly, with progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, which may begin at the site of the wound. The patient gradually falls into a coma and eventually dies. Because of its atypical symptoms, such as the aggressive form, paralytic rabies can be misdiagnosed, leading to the risk of missed cases or incomplete statistics. Proper treatment after being bitten or scratched by an animal. Proper wound treatment and vaccination can effectively prevent rabies (Photo: My Huyen). According to medical recommendations, rabies can be effectively prevented with post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) if the exposed person receives timely treatment before the virus enters the central nervous system and causes disease. You may also like Immediately after being bitten or scratched by a dog, cat, or animal suspected of having rabies, people should thoroughly wash the wound with soap under clean running water for at least 15 minutes. Afterward, they should go to a medical facility as soon as possible for risk assessment and advice on appropriate preventive measures. Depending on the level of exposure and vaccination history, the doctor will prescribe rabies vaccine according to the prescribed schedule. In necessary cases, the patient may be prescribed additional rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) injections to provide protective antibodies at the exposure site. The Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC) advises people not to be complacent, wait for symptoms to appear before seeking medical attention, or self-treat with folk remedies. Once clinical symptoms of rabies appear, the chances of saving the patient are very low. Besides not missing post-exposure prophylaxis, rabies vaccination must also be administered as directed. Dr. Le Thi Giao Thi, from the Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, said that many people are still concerned that the rabies vaccine may affect memory or long-term health. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), current rabies vaccines are primarily inactivated vaccines, produced using cell culture technology or embryonic egg technology. These vaccines have been proven safe and effective in preventing rabies and are recommended by the WHO as a replacement for vaccines produced from nerve tissue due to their higher safety profile. Safety monitoring data indicates that modern rabies vaccines are generally well tolerated. Post-vaccination reactions are mostly mild and transient, such as pain and swelling at the injection site or some mild systemic symptoms. Dr. Thi emphasized that people should not delay or refuse vaccination when indicated due to concerns about side effects. Proper wound management, vaccination, and the use of anti-rabies immunoglobulin as prescribed are important measures to help prevent the virus from causing the disease. "If wounds are treated properly and rabies vaccines and antiserum are administered as prescribed within the appropriate timeframe, the body will develop immunity to prevent the virus from developing, thereby effectively preventing rabies," Dr. Thi shared. About five months ago, the child was bitten on the leg by a neighbor's dog. Two months later, the child was bitten on the ear by another stray dog. However, on both occasions, the family did not take the child to a medical facility for wound treatment or rabies vaccination. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Vaccines Book Vet Visits On September 6th, the child appeared tired and lethargic. The following morning, the child had seizures and was rushed to the emergency room before being transferred to the Gia Lai Provincial Obstetrics and Pediatrics Hospital. There, doctors diagnosed rabies. The family requested to take the child home, where the child subsequently died. Find Pet Care A young man died of rabies two months after being bitten by a dog, without receiving a rabies vaccine (Photo: Getty). Find Pet Care About two months ago, the Department of Health of Dong Thap province reported the case of a 4-year-old girl, NPAN, residing in Dao Thanh ward, who died from rabies after allegedly being bitten by a dog. According to the investigation, on July 4th, while visiting her maternal grandparents in My Phuoc Tay ward, the child suddenly started crying loudly. The family discovered a wound about 6cm long on the child's forehead, bleeding profusely. A dog ran nearby, but it could not be determined whether the child had been bitten by the dog. The child was taken to a local hospital to have the wound stitched up. Because the family did not report a suspected dog bite, the child was not advised to receive rabies vaccine and antiserum. The next day, the family took the child to a vaccination center for consultation, but they refused to administer the rabies vaccine. On August 13th, the child was hospitalized in critical condition, experiencing seizures and motor disturbances. After several transfers to other hospitals, doctors discovered suspected dog bite marks on the forehead. Notably, two saliva tests both returned positive results for the rabies virus. You may also like The child's condition continued to worsen, and he was diagnosed with aggressive rabies, accompanied by respiratory failure and numerous complications. On the evening of August 22nd, the family requested to take the child home. The child died at home that same day. Find Pet Care 100% mortality rate once symptoms appear. According to the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), rabies is a dangerous infectious disease caused by a virus, transmitted from animals to humans. The disease has a nearly 100% mortality rate once clinical symptoms appear, but it is completely preventable if treated and vaccinated promptly after exposure. Each year, rabies claims the lives of tens of thousands of people worldwide . Notably, approximately 40% of victims are children under 15 years old. Dogs are the primary source of rabies virus transmission, accounting for about 99% of human rabies cases. Rabies can infect all mammals, from common pets like dogs, cats, and cattle to wild animals. The rabies virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the saliva of infected animals, most commonly through bites or scratches. The virus can also enter the body when the saliva of an infected animal comes into direct contact with the mucous membranes of the eyes, mouth, or open wounds. The incubation period for rabies typically lasts from two to three months, but can range from one week to one year. This timeframe depends on several factors, including the location of the wound, the extent of the injury, and the amount of virus that enters the body. In the early stages, the disease often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, pain, or an unusual tingling, stinging, or burning sensation at the wound site. When the virus spreads to the central nervous system, the patient may develop encephalitis or myelitis, and the condition can quickly become critical. Find Treatments Rabies in humans is generally divided into two main forms. The aggressive form can cause hyperactivity, agitation, hallucinations, hydrophobia, aerophobia, and unusual behavioral changes. Patients usually die within a few days due to cardiac or respiratory arrest. Meanwhile, paralytic rabies accounts for about 20% of human rabies cases. This form of the disease usually progresses more slowly, with progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, which may begin at the site of the wound. The patient gradually falls into a coma and eventually dies. Because of its atypical symptoms, such as the aggressive form, paralytic rabies can be misdiagnosed, leading to the risk of missed cases or incomplete statistics. Proper treatment after being bitten or scratched by an animal. Proper wound treatment and vaccination can effectively prevent rabies (Photo: My Huyen). According to medical recommendations, rabies can be effectively prevented with post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) if the exposed person receives timely treatment before the virus enters the central nervous system and causes disease. You may also like Immediately after being bitten or scratched by a dog, cat, or animal suspected of having rabies, people should thoroughly wash the wound with soap under clean running water for at least 15 minutes. Afterward, they should go to a medical facility as soon as possible for risk assessment and advice on appropriate preventive measures. Depending on the level of exposure and vaccination history, the doctor will prescribe rabies vaccine according to the prescribed schedule. In necessary cases, the patient may be prescribed additional rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) injections to provide protective antibodies at the exposure site. The Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC) advises people not to be complacent, wait for symptoms to appear before seeking medical attention, or self-treat with folk remedies. Once clinical symptoms of rabies appear, the chances of saving the patient are very low. Besides not missing post-exposure prophylaxis, rabies vaccination must also be administered as directed. Dr. Le Thi Giao Thi, from the Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, said that many people are still concerned that the rabies vaccine may affect memory or long-term health. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), current rabies vaccines are primarily inactivated vaccines, produced using cell culture technology or embryonic egg technology. These vaccines have been proven safe and effective in preventing rabies and are recommended by the WHO as a replacement for vaccines produced from nerve tissue due to their higher safety profile. Safety monitoring data indicates that modern rabies vaccines are generally well tolerated. Post-vaccination reactions are mostly mild and transient, such as pain and swelling at the injection site or some mild systemic symptoms. Dr. Thi emphasized that people should not delay or refuse vaccination when indicated due to concerns about side effects. Proper wound management, vaccination, and the use of anti-rabies immunoglobulin as prescribed are important measures to help prevent the virus from causing the disease. "If wounds are treated properly and rabies vaccines and antiserum are administered as prescribed within the appropriate timeframe, the body will develop immunity to prevent the virus from developing, thereby effectively preventing rabies," Dr. Thi shared. (WBFF) — A cat found in Rosedale tested positive for rabies on Monday, according to the Baltimore County Department of Health and Human Services. The animal is described as an adult, female, domestic short hair, brown tabby with white. ALSO READ | Man wanted in connection with Baltimore County pool parties arrested in North Carolina Now, health officials are urging anyone who may have had contact with the animal to seek immediate medical attention from their healthcare provider or a hospital emergency room (ER). Also, if you or your pet came into direct contact with the rabid cat and sustained bites, scratches and/or licks to contact the Baltimore County Department of Health. Call 410-887-5963 during normal business hours and call 410-832-7182 outside of normal business hours (after 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and on weekends). Powered By 10 Sec Teens charged in deadly east Baltimore crash, grandma demands justice for Eric Browner Jr. Next Stay Health officials are sharing the potential dangers of feeding or touching stray or unknown animals and providing the following rabies prevention tips: Consider the risk of rabies and other diseases before interacting with all animals, especially if the home contains children, people with certain illnesses, elderly, or other pets. Avoid contact with wildlife as well as stray or feral animals, especially if they appear to be sick. Since rabies remains uncontrolled in the wild, there is no risk-free contact with these animals with regard to physical injury, rabies and other diseases.
